procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated November 28, 1966, of the Mysore High Court in Criminal Petition No. 610 of 1966, dismissing the appellant's petition for special leave to appeal against the acquittal of the third accused by the Sessions Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The appellant filed a complaint against the third respondent in the Magistrate's Court.
2. The Magistrate inquired into the case initiated by the appellant's complaint and another case together, and committed the first two respondents and the third respondent separately to the Court of Sessions.
3. The Sessions Judge acquitted all three respondents.
4. The appellant applied to the Mysore High Court under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for special leave to appeal against the acquittal of the three respondents.
5. The High Court dismissed the petition on November 28, 1966, holding that the appellant had no locus standi to prefer an appeal when the State had prosecuted the respondents in the Sessions Court.
6. A revision application filed by the appellant was also rejected.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's order dismissing his petition for special leave to appeal the acquittal. The Supreme Court held that the appellant was entitled to a hearing of his petition for special leave under s. 417(3) and remitted the case to the High Court for this purpose.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant, in a case instituted upon his complaint which was tried jointly with a police-instituted case, has the locus standi under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to file a petition for special leave to appeal against the acquittal.

facts: Two separate cases were tried jointly by a Sessions Court.
One case was instituted by the police against two respondents.
The other case was instituted by the appellant upon his own complaint against a third respondent.
The Sessions Court acquitted all three respondents in both cases.
The appellant then applied to the High Court for special leave to appeal the acquittals under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The High Court dismissed the petition, ruling that the appellant had no 'locus standi' (standing) because the State had prosecuted the respondents in the Sessions Court.
law: The central legal provision is Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
This section grants a complainant the right to apply for special leave to appeal an acquittal, but only if the acquittal was passed in a "case instituted upon complaint."
application: The Supreme Court's decision hinged on whether the appellant's case met the requirement of being a "case instituted upon complaint."
The Court observed that even though the two cases were tried together, they did not merge and their separate identities were maintained throughout the trial.
The acquittal was recorded separately in each of the two distinct cases.
Therefore, the acquittal in the case against the third respondent was, in fact, an acquittal in a case that was instituted upon the appellant's complaint.
Because this essential condition of Section 417(3) was met, the appellant had the right to file the petition.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was entitled to file a petition for special leave to appeal under Section 417(3) because the acquittal was passed in a case that was instituted upon his complaint. The Court found that the joint trial did not extinguish the separate identity of his complaint case, thus giving him the necessary locus standi. The case was sent back to the High Court for a hearing on the merits of the petition.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant, in a case instituted upon his complaint which was tried jointly with a police-instituted case, has the locus standi under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to file a petition for special leave to appeal against the acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The case instituted on the appellant's complaint and the one instituted on the police report were two distinct cases.
There was no merger of the two cases; their separate identities were maintained throughout the trial.
The appellant's case proceeded on its own number, and the acquittal was recorded separately in each of the two cases.
Because his case remained a distinct 'case instituted upon complaint', he was entitled to move the High Court for special leave to appeal the acquittal under Section 417(3) Cr.P.C.
respondent_arguments: The appellant (petitioner) has no locus standi to prefer an appeal.
The State had prosecuted the respondents in the Sessions Court, which negates the private complainant's right to appeal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellant's statutory right to move the High Court is not lost or otherwise affected by the fact that they previously filed a revision application that was rejected.
obiter: In criminal jurisdiction, the word 'case' ordinarily means a proceeding for the prosecution of a person alleged to have committed an offence, which results in either a discharge, conviction, or acquittal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a case instituted upon a private complaint is tried jointly with a case instituted on a police report, there is no merger of the two cases if their separate identities are maintained throughout the trial. If the complainant's case proceeds on its own number and the acquittal is recorded separately, it remains a 'case instituted upon complaint', and the complainant is therefore entitled under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to move the High Court for special leave to appeal the acquittal.
legal_tests_applied: The court determined whether a case qualifies as one 'instituted upon complaint' for the purposes of Section 417(3) by examining if its procedural identity remained distinct from a jointly tried police-instituted case, specifically by checking if it proceeded on its own case number and if the final judgment of acquittal was recorded separately for it.
policy_considerations: A complainant's statutory right to move the High Court for special leave to appeal an acquittal cannot be lost or negated simply because their complaint-case was tried jointly with a police-instituted case or because a separate application for revision was rejected.
